chapters.title: The Fait Accompli Strategy: Take Small Bites

chapterBreakdown.gentle: Oriana stops bringing the whole operating overhaul into one meeting. Each time she presents the full shift, people see the scale at once and line up against it. She changes method instead. One smaller approval adjusts reporting. Another resets review timing. Another narrows who must sign off. Each step looks manageable on its own, so the room lets it pass. Greene's fait accompli strategy works through that mismatch between local judgment and aggregate effect. People often weigh each bite separately and miss what the bites become together. Dashiell pushes that point in a graduate-public-administration-seminar when classmates treat incrementalism as automatically harmless. He asks what the sequence adds up to and whether anyone would object if the total aim were stated plainly at the start.
chapterBreakdown.direct: Oriana stops asking for one large process change because one large request triggers organized resistance. She breaks the move into smaller approvals instead. A reporting adjustment passes. A schedule change passes. A sign-off change passes. None looks big enough to justify a major fight. Together they deliver most of the original result. That is the fait accompli strategy. The operator stays below reaction threshold until the aggregate position is already built. Dashiell gives the classroom correction in a graduate-public-administration-seminar. Small steps are not innocent by default. The real test is cumulative. What do the moves add up to, and would the affected people still consent if the full sequence were named at the beginning? Honest sequencing survives that question. Concealed accumulation does not.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: Oriana quits asking for the whole prize in one shot. A big proposal wakes the room up, so she starts taking slices instead. One minor approval alters reporting lines. Another shifts review timing. Another moves decision rights. Nobody wants a full fight over any single slice, so the slices keep landing. By the time opponents total the damage, the field has already moved. That is Greene's fait accompli strategy. You gain by building position under the level that triggers full resistance. Dashiell strips away the classroom excuse in a graduate-public-administration-seminar. Small is not the same as harmless. If the sequence would draw real opposition once aggregated, then hiding the total is not patience. It is cover.

point.gentle: Small moves can accumulate into a major change before others fully register the total.
point.direct: Opponents often miss the aggregate when they judge each step alone.
point.competitive: Win the ground in slices before the other side counts the loss.

point.gentle: Reaction thresholds are usually set for one visible event, not for a quiet sequence.
point.direct: A minor move can pass because it looks beneath the cost of resistance.
point.competitive: Most defenses are calibrated for a punch, not a steady bite pattern.

point.gentle: The ethical line appears when smallness is used to hide a total outcome people would reject in full view.
point.direct: Read cumulative consent, not just local permission.
point.competitive: If the hidden total would start a war, do not pretend each bite was neutral.

oneMinuteRecap.gentle: The fait accompli strategy builds large change through small approvals that stay under reaction threshold until the total becomes hard to reverse.
oneMinuteRecap.direct: Break the move into pieces, but judge the strategy by the aggregate result rather than by each isolated step.
oneMinuteRecap.competitive: Take ground in bites, not lunges, and keep asking whether the hidden total would trigger a real counterattack if exposed.

chapterBreakdown.gentle: Oriana gives up on the dramatic version of the change. Every time she asks for the full operating shift, resistance forms early because everyone can see the total loss of comfort, autonomy, and control. She changes the tempo instead of the objective. A smaller reporting adjustment looks procedural. A revised review cadence looks temporary. A narrowed sign-off path looks efficient. Each step feels easier to tolerate than the whole. Greene's fait accompli strategy depends on that local-reading habit. People often ask whether this move is worth fighting, not what several accepted moves will become once they lock together. The result is cumulative change that reaches solidity before opponents react at full scale. Dashiell names the missing test in a graduate-public-administration-seminar. Incrementalism is not morally clean just because it is incremental. The honest question is whether each step stays defensible even after the full sequence is visible. If the total must stay obscured to survive resistance, then the strategy has moved from disciplined sequencing into concealed cumulative pressure.
chapterBreakdown.direct: The fait accompli strategy is cumulative sequencing below reaction threshold. Oriana learns that one large proposal creates one large coalition against her, so she stops presenting the whole design. She routes the change through several smaller approvals that look operational rather than transformational. Reviewers assess each request locally. They ask whether this one adjustment is worth the cost of a fight. Because the answer keeps coming back no, the approvals stack. By the time anyone totals reporting shifts, cadence changes, and sign-off transfers, the operating model has already changed. Dashiell provides the chapter's corrective frame in a graduate-public-administration-seminar. Small steps are not automatically legitimate. The proper audit is aggregate. What does the sequence produce, who absorbs the cost, and would the same people accept the plan if the whole path were disclosed in advance? This strategy is practical when the sequence remains defensible under full disclosure. It becomes manipulative when fragmentation is used to prevent informed opposition to the cumulative result.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: Oriana stops trying to win the war in one meeting because a visible land grab invites a visible defense. She starts collecting ground in smaller bites. A reporting tweak slides through. A schedule change slides through. A sign-off revision slides through. Each move looks too minor to justify mobilization, but the sequence is doing real territorial work. That is the point of the fait accompli strategy. You exploit the gap between how people price single events and how little they monitor accumulation. Once the structure is built in parts, reversal costs go up because the new reality is spread across several settled decisions instead of one headline fight. Dashiell kills the lazy classroom reading in a graduate-public-administration-seminar. Small is not innocent. If you need the total aim to stay blurry because the whole would trigger justified resistance, then the sequence is functioning as cover. Strong operators track that distinction because salami tactics buy leverage fast and legitimacy slowly, and legitimacy is what explodes when the concealed total finally becomes visible.

chapterBreakdown.gentle: Oriana's success depends less on persuasion than on institutional pacing. She notices that reviewers are not evaluating her objective in the abstract. They are evaluating whether each discrete request is disruptive enough to justify resistance now. That difference gives her room. A reporting adjustment framed as housekeeping, a cadence revision framed as efficiency, and a sign-off change framed as de-bottlenecking all move through separate gates with lower perceived stakes than the unified plan would carry. Greene's fait accompli strategy lives inside that administrative fragmentation. The cumulative result becomes sturdy because it is distributed across approvals that each developed their own little normality. Dashiell slows the chapter down in a graduate-public-administration-seminar by forcing an aggregate reading. He asks who benefits from evaluating the sequence locally and who bears the cost when nobody totals it until late. That is the ethical fault line. Staged implementation can be legitimate when capacity limits, learning needs, and risk control make phasing sensible. It turns unstable when the operator relies on compartmentalization to smuggle through a total outcome that could not survive honest naming, informed consent, and whole-plan scrutiny.
chapterBreakdown.direct: The hard lesson in the fait accompli strategy is not merely that small moves pass more easily. It is that institutions often separate approval, memory, and accountability. Oriana exploits that architecture. She does not need every reviewer to agree with the final operating design. She needs each reviewer to see one request that appears tolerable within that reviewer's narrow mandate. A reporting change looks administrative. A cadence change looks procedural. A sign-off transfer looks like throughput management. Because no single gate owns the combined shift, the sequence advances. That is why the defense cannot be emotional suspicion alone. It has to be structural aggregation: tracking linked approvals, shared beneficiaries, directional drift, and the moment when separate concessions form one integrated shift. Dashiell names the governance question clearly in a graduate-public-administration-seminar. Would the affected people consent if the full pathway were declared at the start? If yes, sequencing may be disciplined implementation. If no, fragmentation is doing political work by suppressing informed resistance. The operator who ignores that line may still win the sequence but will inherit backlash, legitimacy loss, and a field that remembers the gain as procedural bad faith.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: Salami tactics work because most organizations guard the headline move and neglect the campaign ledger. Oriana reads that weakness correctly. She stops asking for the obvious conquest and instead feeds the system a run of requests that seem too technical, too local, or too cheap to contest hard. Separate reviewers process separate bites. Nobody spends coalition energy on any single one. Then the structure closes. Reporting now flows differently, timing now favors her camp, and decision rights now sit closer to her side. That is a positional win built through administrative underreaction. The hard edge is what comes next. Dashiell points out in a graduate-public-administration-seminar that accumulation and concealment are not the same thing, but they often travel together. Once the total aim depends on nobody summing the parts, the operator has shifted from disciplined sequencing into covert leverage. That can still work tactically. It also loads the field with grievance, retrospective anger, and counter-mobilization once opponents finally assemble the map. If you use the bite chain, know whether you are buying implementation runway or merely postponing the war until the bill gets larger.
